::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false" title="Purpose"}
This assignment focuses on Step 3 of the five-step hypothesis-testing process:
selecting a test and translating a statistical story into null and alternative
hypotheses.

You will choose three project hypotheses, select an appropriate inferential test
for each one, and develop pseudocode describing your intended analysis. You are
planning the analysis, not running tests or producing results yet.
:::

## Objectives

By the end of this assignment, you will be able to:

- distinguish among the inferential tests introduced in the course;
- match a test to the variables and study design;
- state $H_0$ and $H_A$ in context; and
- outline data-loading, filtering, and testing steps as R pseudocode.

## 1) Review the Available Tests

| Function | Test | Typical structure |
|---|---|---|
| `csf()` | Chi-square goodness-of-fit test | One categorical variable |
| `csi()` | Chi-square test of independence | Two categorical variables |
| `ost()` | One-sample t-test | One numeric variable vs a reference value |
| `idt()` | Independent-samples t-test | Numeric outcome by two independent groups |
| `idw()` | Wilcoxon rank-sum test | Numeric/ordinal outcome by two independent groups |
| `pst()` | Paired-samples t-test | Numeric outcome measured in pairs |
| `psw()` | Wilcoxon signed-rank test | Numeric/ordinal outcome measured in pairs |
| `ano()` | One-way ANOVA | Numeric outcome by three or more groups |
| `slr()` | Simple linear regression | Numeric outcome and one numeric predictor |

Select a test based on the variables, number of groups, independence or pairing,
and the type of comparison in your statistical story.

---

## 2) Review the Worked Example

### Statistical story

For recorded Chicago crashes, does the mean number of reported injuries per
crash differ between **Daytime** and **Night or early morning**? A safety team
could use this question to plan a closer review of when injury burden occurs.

### Estimate or plot to plan

Plan a comparison of the mean `injuries_total` in each of the two `time_period`
groups, along with their group sizes and distributions. Describe what you would
look for; do not calculate or report the results for this homework.

### Test and hypotheses

The outcome is numeric and the comparison uses two separate groups, so the
starting plan is an independent-samples t-test using `idt()`. Before running
it later, check the sampling design, independence, and the distribution of
injury counts; the variable may contain many zeros and be strongly skewed.

$H_0$: The population mean number of reported injuries per recorded crash is
the same for Daytime and Night or early morning.

$H_A$: Those population mean injury counts differ.

$\alpha = 0.05$

### Pseudocode with an optional commented R draft

The first part describes the plan in plain language. The second part shows how
that plan might begin to become R code. Both remain comments; you do not need
to execute the code or produce a test result.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# PSEUDOCODE
# Read data/traffic_chicago_2024.csv.
# Keep Daytime and Night or early morning crashes.
# Exclude records with missing injuries_total or time_period.
# Plan a check of group sizes, injury distributions, and independence.
# Compare mean injuries_total between the two groups with an appropriate test.

# OPTIONAL R DRAFT: leave commented out for this homework.
# crashes <- readr::read_csv("data/traffic_chicago_2024.csv")
# planned_data <- crashes |>
#   dplyr::filter(
#     time_period %in% c("Daytime", "Night or early morning"),
#     !is.na(injuries_total)
#   )
# planned_test <- planned_data |>
#   eco230r::idt(injuries_total ~ time_period)
```

Missing injuries are not automatically zero. This is a comparison of recorded
crashes, not a claim that time of day causes injuries or that the sample
represents every road user. Steps 4-5, test execution, and statistical/practical
interpretations of results come later.
